SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
BASIS OF CERTIFICATION
The Emergency Flotation and Life Raft System is approved for ditching,
up to Sea State 6, in accordance with JAR/FAR 29.
The Emergency Flotation System P/N 4G9560F00111 and
4G9560F00211 are approved for ditching , up to Sea State 6, in
accordance with JAR/FAR 29 provided the following approved
equipments, in accordance with the National Operation rules, are
fitted:
— Life preservers.
TYPE OF OPERATIONS
For flight over water the helicopter must be operated in accordance
with the National Operating rules.
The approved cabin layouts are detailed in Section 6 of this
Supplement and in Section 6 of the Basic RFM and appropriate
Supplement.
WEIGHT AND CENTER OF GRAVITY LIMITATION
After installation of the DART Emergency Flotation System the new
empty weight and center of gravity position must be determined.
No change to weight or CG limitations.
TAKE OFF LIMITATIONS
Take off after ditching is prohibited.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
MISCELLANEOUS LIMITATIONS
Flotation System
The Emergency Flotation system shall only be used for ditching.
Flotation bags shall not be inflated in flight.
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S95-7
Rev. 30

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND MALFUNCTION
PROCEDURES
EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
DITCHING
Consideration should be given to the environmental factors, such as
wind direction and speed, sea state and engine power available.
Approach and landing should be into wind.
When landing into waves, land head-on to oncoming waves avoiding,
if possible, ditching into the face of the wave.
WARNING
As considerable error can result from estimation of height
over water, the radar altimeter should be used for height
cues during descent.
WARNING
Do not deploy flotation bags in flight. Bags will automati-
cally deploy on water touchdown.
CAUTION
At high touchdown speeds, the rotorcraft may roll and
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters turn to the left after touchdown due to gyroscopic effects.
This will require pilot corrective action.
Note
After ditching the rotor brake does not func-
tion, even if the undercarriage is extended.
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S95-15
Rev. 19

DITCHING PROCEDURES - AEO
1. Pre-ditching checks — Warn crew and passengers to
prepare for ditching.
2. OFF/ARMED switch — Confirm ARMED. FLOAT ARM
(FLOATS EMER panel) caution displayed on CAS.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
3. Landing Gear — Confirm UP.
CAUTION
If the landing gear cannot be retracted, ditching with min-
imum forward speed is recommended.
4. Lights — At night, switch ON emergency
lights and landing light.
5. Landing direction — If possible orientate the aircraft
for an approach into the
prevailing wind.
6. Brief — Cabin crew and occupants.
7. Radar altimeter — Verify working.
8. Windscreen wipers — Select FAST.
9. Distress procedure — Broadcast Mayday.
10. Initial point — During the approach, reduce
airspeed gradually to arrive at a
position 200 ft (60 m) above
touchdown point with a rate of
descent of no more than 500
fpm. Initiate a deceleration to
achieve 30 kts at 50 ft (15 m) . At
50 ft (15 m) rotate nose up to
approximately 20° to decelerate.

AUTOROTATIVE LANDING PROCEDURE ON WATER
In the event of a ditching being required following a twin engine failure
the approach and ditching should be carried out as follows:
1. Collective pitch — Smoothly and rapidly reduce to
enter autorotation.
2. Cyclic — Adjust to obtain autorotation
speed between 80 KIAS
(minimum rate of descent
speed) and 100 KIAS (Best
range speed).
3. Collective pitch — Adjust to obtain up to 110% NR.
4. OFF/ARMED switch — Confirm ARMED. FLOAT ARM
(FLOATS EMER panel) caution displayed on CAS.
5. Landing gear — Confirm UP.
CAUTION
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters If the landing gear cannot be retracted, ditching with
minimum forward speed is recommended.
6. Landing direction — Select and manoeuvre into wind
7. Brief — Cabin crew and occupants.
8. Radar altimeter — Verify working.
9. Windscreen wipers — Select FAST.

GENERAL INFORMATION
The Heavy Duty Baggage Compartment Kit consists of an optional kit
that is installed in the baggage compartment area to allow all of the
baggage bay volume to be used for baggage.
The kit consist of barrier panels and vertical nets around the baggage
bay area. This permits the baggage to be loaded without the require-
ment for a restraint net. The vertical nets are connected to attach-
ments on the baggage bay floor and ceiling.
Heavy Duty Baggage Compartment Kit permits baggage to be loaded
up to the cabin/tunnel dividing barrier utilizing 3 zones. Two additional
internal dividing nets are also mounted in the baggage bay area
between Zone 1, Zone 2 and Zone 3. See Figure 2. Zone 3 is
intended for personal items only.
This configuration is compatible with the Auxiliary Fuel Tank (Supple-
ment 15).
The dividing nets used in the Heavy Duty Baggage Compartment can
be seen in Figure 2. To load/unload baggage these nets must be un-
hooked, as required, to load the baggage in the appropriate zone,
then re-attached for flight. No further securing is required for baggage.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S96-1

DEFINITIONS
1. Take Off Decision Point (TDP) — The first point in the Take-Off
path from which a CTO
capability is assured and the
last point from which a RTO is
assured, within the rejected Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
take off distance.
2. Continued Take Off distance — The horizontal distance from
the start of the take off
procedure to a point at least
where V TOSS and a positive rate
of climb are attained following
an engine failure at or after
TDP.
3. Rejected Take Off distance — The horizontal distance from
the start of the take off
procedure to a point where
the helicopter lands and stops
safely following an engine
failure prior to TDP.
4. PATH 1 - PATH 2 — The segment between the end
of the CTO distance (or BL
distance) to a height of 1000 ft
(300 m) ATS during an OEI
2.5 min power climb at V COSS
for a minimum ROC of 600 fpm.
5. Take Off Safety Speed (V TOSS ) — The airspeed at which 100 fpm
rate of climb is assured.
6. Climb Out Safety Speed V COSS — The airspeed at which the
scheduled climb gradient OEI
can be achieved.
7. Elevated Heliport — A heliport which is at least 3 m
(10 ft) above the surrounding
surface.

Supplement 97 AW139 - RFM - 4D
CAT A Enhanced Document N°
Offshore Procedure 139G0290X002
GENERAL
This supplement details an Enhanced Offshore Elevated Helideck
Take-Off procedure permitting an improved WAT for the take-off.
For Landing Procedures see appropriate Part in Supplement 12.
The Take-Off technique requires the Pilot Flying (PF) and Pilot Not
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
Flying (PNF) coordinate their activities so that the PNF will monitor the
height and call out Take Off Decision Point (TDP) and, in the case of
engine failure, the rotor speed (NR) allowing the PF to concentrate on
flying the manoeuvres.
The technique uses a vertical climb at 400 to 500 fpm (using 25%
Delta PI) above the helideck to achieve a TDP height of 25 ft (7.5 m)
where a nose down rotation commences for the flyaway. An engine
failure before TDP means the vertical climb must be stopped and the
aircraft rejected back to the helideck (RTO). An engine failure at or
after the TDP means the pilot must continue the rotation for a Contin-
ued Take Off (CTO) on one engine (OEI). This Take-Off procedure
also assures a deck edge clearance (always exceeding 15 ft (5 m)
vertical and 35 ft horizontal), even when the manoeuvre requires a
drop down Below the Take Off Surface (BTS).
The Take-Off manoeuvre is commenced with the helicopter nose
wheel between 1.5 m and 4.0 m from the edge of the helideck.
When operating at the condition given in the Weight, Altitude, Temper-
ature (WAT) chart below, the technique above always assures no
exposure time to a ditching in case of an engine failure.
If the Take-Off WAT weight is such that in case of an engine failure a
drop down is required it is assumed that the height of the Elevated
Helideck is greater than the Drop Down plus a height clearance mar-
gin, as required by the Competent Authorities, and that there are no
obstacles beyond and below the deck edge.
Page S97-4 E.A.S.A. Approved
Rev. 21

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND MALFUNCTION
PROCEDURES
GENERAL TAKE - OFF
The procedures detailed herein only consider the failure of one engine
in the Take-Off path and assume the pilot gives first priority to aircraft
control and to achieve a safe flight path.
For the Take-Off procedure the following shall be observed:
1. Engine failure prior to TDP — Recognition of engine failure
prior to the TDP dictates that
the Take-Off be rejected.
2. Engine failure at or after TDP — Recognition of the failure at or
after the TDP dictates that the
Take-Off be continued.
Procedures dealing with subsequent Failure/Malfunctions, other than
engine failure, must be initiated only after the aircraft control and a
safe flight/ground condition have been obtained. The procedures for
the emergency/malfunction can be followed according to the appropri-
ate instructions detailed in Section 3 of the basic Rotorcraft Flight
Manual.
TAKE OFF PROCEDURES
For Take-Off the PNF should monitor engine and rotor parameters and
make the following calls:
— TDP

— Approaching 25 kts

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
WIND EFFECT
For Crosswind and Headwind Benefit Component refer to Wind
Component Chart (Figure 1-2) to define if wind benefit is applicable.
For Azimuths between 20° and 90° and windspeed below 15 kts no
wind benefit is applicable.
For Azimuths between 20° and 90° and windspeed above 15 kts refer
to Wind Component Chart Figure 4-13 for Crosswind and Headwind
Benefit computation.
For Azimuths between -90° and 20° full windspeed is applicable for
wind benefit computation.

DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS
Abbreviations and acronyms used throughout this Supplement are
defined as follows:
— BQRS : Backup Quick Release System
— HEC : Human External Cargo
— NHEC : Non Human External Cargo
— PCDS : Personnel Carrying Device System
— PQRS : Primary Quick Release System
GENERAL INFORMATION
This supplement details the use of the DUAL CARGO HOOK
installation for HEC operations.
The dual cargo hook system P/N 4G2592F00111 introduces a
secondary cargo hook mounted in front of the already certified main
cargo hook (refer Supplement 13). See Figure 1 & Figure 2.
The main cargo hook, during normal operation, takes the suspended
load and only in the case of an inadvertent release from the main hook
the load is then supported by the secondary hook.
The Dual Cargo Hook system therefore consists of:
— the Main Hook (P/N 3G2592F00111)
— the Secondary hook
— the DUAL HOOK control panel (fitted in the interseat control
panel)
— Primary and Secondary Quick Release Systems for the Main and
Secondary Hook
— ‘Y’ shaped long line (for HEC use) and safety harness.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
The main hook P/N 3G2592F00111 has a support frame assembly, a
cargo hook assembly and a hook load indicator mounted in the cockpit
(Figure 9). The hook has a PQRS via a guarded pushbutton on the
pilot and copilot cyclic (Figure 7). A secondary manual release
system, for operation by ground personnel only, is mounted on the
cargo hook. An Emergency Cargo Release (MAIN EMER) guarded
switch, located on the DUAL HOOK control panel in the interseat
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S98-1
Rev. 23

=== DOC PAGE 3646 ===
Supplement 98 AW139 - RFM - 4D
Dual Cargo Hook Document N°
Operations 139G0290X002
console, that operates an electrical explosive cartridge to release the
load.
The secondary hook is mounted on a dedicated frame which is
attached to the fuselage, in front of the main hook. The hook has a
normal load release (PQRS) which is hydraulically operated via
double action levers located on the pilot collective stick (Figure 8). To
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
open the hook, the pilot must lower the yellow locking lever then pull
the red release lever. A secondary manual release system, for
operation by ground personnel only, is mounted on the cargo hook (a
protection plate prevents inadvertent operation of the manual release
Figure 5). An Emergency Cargo Release (SEC EMER) guarded
switch, located on the DUAL HOOK control panel in the interseat
console, operates an electrical rotary solenoid to release the load.
Once the secondary hook has been opened, by any of the means,
then it must be closed manually and confirmed, using the lock
indicators on the side of the hook, that it is closed correctly, see
Figure 6.
When the system is selected ON using the PWR switch on the DUAL
HOOK control panel (Figure 4) the system status is indicated by CAS
cautions. The HOOK ARM caution illuminates if any of the CARGO
REL switch guards on either cyclic is opened or the MAIN EMERG or
SEC EMERG guards are opened on the DUAL HOOK control panel.
The HOOK OPEN caution illuminates when the main cargo hook is
opened by the following methods:
• holding depressed either cyclic pushbutton, the hook load arm
opens releasing the load. When the pushbutton has been
released, a spring in the cargo hook assembly closes the load arm
back to its closed and latched position (caution no longer
illuminated),
or
• pressing the MAIN EMERG pushbutton the electrical explosive
system allows the hook load arm to open releasing the load. A
spring in the cargo hook assembly automatically closes the load
arm back to its closed (but not latched) position (caution no longer
illuminated),
or
• when opened manually on the ground.
Page S98-2 E.A.S.A. Approved
Rev. 23

The secondary hook does not produce a hook open caution for either
the PQRS or the SEC EMER release.
For HEC operations the load is suspended to the helicopter by a
Y shaped Long Line connected to the main and secondary hook by
two separate cable ends. The main hook end is the shorter one, so
that in normal operations the load is sustained by the main hook only
and the line attached to the secondary hook is slack.
A kit of two monitoring cameras (P/N 3G9770F00111) which display
images of load movement and hook condition on the MFD, and/or the
5th display (if fitted), is available. The monitoring cameras are
operated by a switch on the Auxiliary Circuit Breaker Panel
( Figure 12 ).

‘Y’ SHAPED LONG LINE
The Y shaped Long Line (Figure 10) intended for HEC operation
consists of the first segment of the Long Line (the Y-shaped part)
which is approximately 18 m long and has one line for the main hook
shorter than the other line for the secondary hook (slack line), and the
swivel part which is approximately 2 m long, therefore the minimum
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
Long Line length is 20 m.
The intermediate segments available are 10 m, 20 m, and 40 m
segment long therefore the total length of the Long Line can vary from
20 m to 90 m with 10 steps depending on customer requirements.
At the bottom end of the Long Line a swivel provides independent
rotation of the load with respect to the Long Line.
The load is attached to the swivel by 4 lugs each one provided by a
carabiner.
An additional attachment tool with 8 carabiners can also be connected
to increase the number of attachment points (Figure 11).

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
NHEC operations must be conducted using only the Main Hook, see
Supplement 13.
The PCDS Long Line part Number 6F2592V01151 is intended for
HEC operations and must not be used for any other type of
operations.
When HEC operations are not envisaged the Secondary hook must be
stowed.
When operations using the Secondary Hook are not required, and the
hook is stowed, refer to Supplement 13 for Cargo Hook Operations
using just the main cargo hook installation (be aware that the DUAL
HOOK control panel labeling for MAIN EMERG is slightly different
from the single hook panel but has exactly the same function).
With the Dual Cargo Hook fitted, but not used, and the hooks are in a
stowed position, the Limitations and Performance stated in the Basic
RFM and applicable Supplements apply.
The Dual Cargo Hook equipment certification approval does NOT
constitute operational approval. Operational approval for external load
operation must be granted by the Competent Aviation Authority.
The Dual Cargo Hook system meets the certification requirements for
HEC operations.
For compliance with operating rules, the AW139 is certified to CAT A
engineering standards.
During HEC cargo Hook operations the number of external load cycles
must be recorded in the helicopter log-book.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters An external load cycle is defined as every external load lift using the
Cargo Hook.
A load cycle is defined as the lifting of at least 1 person with the load
attached to the main hook.

TYPE OF OPERATION
— Dual Cargo Hook operation must be authorized by the Competent
Authority in accordance with the applicable National Operating
Regulations.
— The Dual Cargo hook installation is approved for HEC operations.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
— Dual Cargo hook operation is approved for Day and Night VFR
with ground visual contact.
— Operation of the Dual Cargo Hook equipment for HEC requires the
use of an approved PCDS which has the appropriate size selected
for the mission.
The Y Long Line P/N 6F2592V01151 together with Safety Harness
AMTC-H1037-BL is an approved PCDS for HEC operations.
— For HEC operations there shall be equipment to allow direct inter
communication between the required crew members and the
external occupants. An approved Radio-ICS system must be
installed and operated in accordance with the applicable Local
Operating Regulations.
Polycon P/N 4G2350F02311 is an approved Radio-ICS system.
However, the Radio ICS shall not be the only means of
communication with the Crew/HEC.

AIRSPEED LIMITATIONS WITH HEC
V MAX ....................................................................................... 90 KIAS
WARNING
Operations with an empty PCDS (as with any unballasted
strop) can be extremely dangerous. The most critical
flight condition is forward flight which can result in close
proximity or contact between the PCDS and the aircraft,
especially if other factors such as high rate of descent,
abrupt aircraft manoeuvres or turbulence are present.
Extreme care must be taken when flying with empty
PCDS and flight conditions and manoeuvres must be
limited as necessary to ensure satisfactory PCDS
behaviour in the prevailing atmospheric conditions.
CAUTION
The airspeed with external cargo may be limited by load
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters dynamic characteristics to an airspeed below V .
MAX
Caution should be exercised when carrying external load
to ensure satisfactory load dynamic characteristics,
which may be affected by the size, weight and shape of
the load, as well as by the length of the strop between the
load and the hook. The operator is responsible to
establish adequate operating limits to ensure satisfactory
load dynamics characteristics for the type of load being
carried.

DUAL CARGO HOOK OPERATING PROCEDURES
General
In normal conditions the long line will be attached to the hooks whilst
the helicopter is on ground, at the beginning of the HEC mission. The
human load is attached to (and detached from) the long line by means
of the carabiners provided on the long line lower end. The long line
shall be detached from the hooks at the end of the HEC mission, when
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters the helicopter is on ground, by means of the PQRS or the manual
release systems (to be operated by ground personnel).
The following procedure assumes that the load is attached and
detached while the helicopter is in the hover. Depending on number of
people and sling length being used other techniques may also be
applicable.

SECTION 3 - EMERGENCY AND MALFUNCTION
PROCEDURES
GENERAL
An unexpected thump/impulse/noise from the hook area, possibly
accompanied by an abrupt vertical/pitch disturbance, should be
interpreted as indicating that the primary load connection to the
aircraft has failed, due to either primary hook or PCDS failure resulting
in load transfer to the secondary PCDS cable and secondary hook.
This event may or may not be associated with a HOOK OPEN caution.
If this is confirmed, using the cargo hook monitoring cameras and/or
main hook load indicator reads zero, HEC operations must be
discontinued and the HEC taken to the nearest operationally suitable
safe set down area.
PCDS EMERGENCY JETTISON
An emergency jettison of the PCDS, in flight, should only be carried
out if absolutely necessary, using the following procedure:
1. PWR switch on DUAL HOOK — Confirm ON.
control panel

released.

SECTION 4 - PERFORMANCE DATA
GENERAL
Forward flight and climb performance will be degraded due to the load
aerodynamic drag. The level of degradation will depend on load size
and shape.
There are no significant load effects on hover performance.

SECTION 6 - WEIGHT AND BALANCE
After installation of the Dual Cargo Hook System determined the new
empty weight and center of gravity position.
For DUAL CARGO HOOK operations Longitudinal and Lateral
Moments may be calcuated using:
— the MAIN Cargo Hook positions of STA 5300 mm, BL 0 mm
and
— the Secondary Cargo Hook position of STA 4923mm, BL 0 mm.
These values must be used in the Weight and Balance Calculations to
ensure if the load transfers to the Secondary Cargo Hook the
longitudinal moment remains within the Limitations reported in
Section 1.
See below for examples of CG movement due to HEC transfer from
Main Hook to Secondary hook.

and HEC.

GENERAL INFORMATION
The Cabin Partial Extension with Baggage Barrier Net modification
consists of:
• Removal of the cabin rear dividing panel, from STN 5700 mm
• Installation of a new panel at STN 6700 mm
• Installation of Restraint Net attachments at STN 5795, which
allows the Baggage Barrier Restraint Net (P/N 3G2550A16811) to
be installed
• Tunnel floor and walls reinforced panel installation.
The new area exposed allows the space above/between the main fuel
tanks (Tunnel Stowage Area) to be used as a storage area for non
dangerous, personal items I.A.W. ICAO Annex 18. See Figure 1. The
baggage can be contained in the tunnel area up to a maximum of
370 kg.
When the Partial Cabin Extension is installed and baggage is loaded
the area directly infront of the baggage barrier net is required to be
free of obstacles. Therefore, depending on the cabin layout seats may
need to be removed. to keep the area clear. See Section 6 of this
supplement for information of seating area which is to remain clear
when the tunnel stowage area is being used.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S99-1
Rev. 27

AW139 - RFM - 4D Supplement 100
Document N ° Baggage Compartment
139G0290X002 Restraint System
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement covers the Baggage Compartment Restraint System
which improves the loading and restraint of baggage in the baggage
compartment.
The installation is made up of:
• The Baggage Compartment Restraints System (P/N
4G5340F00311) installs a modified baggage bay floor, at the
same level as the baggage door opening and including a series
of rollers and tied down points which eases the loading and
unloading process
• Cargo Restraint Net P/N 4G2550F00711 and Cargo Anchor
System P/N 4G2550F00811 used to secure the baggage onto
the floor tied down points.
The Baggage Restraint System also requires the installation of the
Baggage Door Extension Kit (P/N 4G5230F00111) which increases
the baggage door opening by 80 mm along the top edge of the door
and installs a new door and a locking mechanism on the front and rear
edge of the door. This kit also include the installation of compatible fire
proof panels around the baggage compartment.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S100-1
Rev. 24

AW139 - RFM - 4D Supplement 101
Document N ° Phase 8 Additional
139G0290X002 Functions
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Primus EPIC Phase 8 provides the following:
1. Additional functions:
— PFD page layout changes
• Expansion of Pitch Tape for conformity with optional SVS
representation.
• Full Blue over Brown (BoB) format to avoid abrupt changes in
PFD layout when activating / deactivating SVS
• Introduction of Path/Pitch Modes to emphasis aircraft flight path
or allow pilots to use legacy Flight Director display positioning
with less emphasis on flight path.
Path mode only available if optional SVS enabled in option file.
— Flight Path Symbol
• To indicate actual path angle of aircraft
• To provide awareness of aircraft path with respect to external
scene depiction on PFD when optional SVS is selected ON.
— 2D Terrain on MFD and PFD HSI
Representation of absolute terrain with various colour shades from
green to brown, depending on terrain absolute elevation above
MSL. Known obstacles are superimposed to the terrain
representation.
— INAV Map on MFD
Interactive Navigation (INAV) map, displaying geopolitical
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
boundaries and other elements (airways, airspaces, airports,
heliports etc.) in surrounding environment with respect to the
aircraft position and flight plan.
— Custom Approach
Custom Approach is an assistance function to help reduce pilot
workload when approaching small airports, airfields, heliports and
oil rigs with a non-published approach procedure.
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S101-1
Rev. 26

=== DOC PAGE 3724 ===
Supplement 101 AW139 - RFM - 4D
Phase 8 Additional Document N°
Functions 139G0290X002
Custom Approach allows the pilot to fly a user defined, flight
director-coupled approach to the active flight plan destination
waypoint (user defined or from the NAV DB).
Custom approaches can be set with or without a final level
segment. When Custom approach with a final level segment is
enabled in the option file, the selection between the type of
approach is made during settings via MCDU. Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
— Cursor Control Device (CCD)
Optimised cursor control device which includes the SVS selection
button (only active if SVS kit installed) and a handgrip joystick.
— Flight Plan Upload - Download
The capability to import and export single flight plans from or to an
external memory device through DLMU-W/ADG-400 interface.
— VTA Annunciation
VTA annunciation is displayed starting at 200 ft above MAP
waypoint when flying with VGP mode engaged.
— Continuation of Performance Calculations After Landing
Once Initialized, the FMS performance computation will keep
operating, without pilot's actions, also after a landing.
— Reduced Leg Length of Leg Search Patterns
Refer Supplement 68 for details.
2. Support to the following:
— Synthetic Vision System (SVS)
This is an optional kit which gives a 3D perspective
representation of the external scene integrated onto the PFD.
Refer Supplement 102.

SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
REQUIRED EQUIPMENT
PRIMUS EPIC Phase 8 Software Release EB7030191-00113/00120.
FMS LIMITATIONS
Upload of Flight Plans from an external device to the FMS selected as
Navigation Source for PFD in command is forbidden.
2D TERRAIN/OBSTACLE LIMITATIONS
The 2D Terrain and Obstacle display on PFD HSI and MFD is
intended to enhance awareness only:
— Navigation shall not be based upon the use of the 2D Terrain/
Obstacle display
— Terrain and obstacle avoidance must not rely upon 2D Terrain/
Obstacle display only.
INAV DATABASE LIMITATIONS
Approval of the Honeywell INAV is based upon Terrain, Obstacle and
Navigation databases from a database provider who has obtained a
Type 2 Letter of Acceptance (LOA). The operator must ensure
compliance with section 13 of AC 20-153B.
The last updated INAV database must be loaded on the displays.
CUSTOM APPROACH LIMITATIONS
Type of Operation
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
— Custom Approach, without level segment, is approved under Day/
Night VFR operation,
— Custom Approach with level segment is approved under DAY/
Night VFR and IFR operation.
The final approach segment must be carried out over water.
— All Custom Approaches must only be flown with FD coupled.

Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters

PFD CHANGES
The PFD layout has an expansion of the pitch scale and the
introduction of a Blue over Brown (BoB) format. See Figure 7-1.
The existing symbology has been slightly adjusted in size,
transparency and location to adapt to the BoB format, the Synthetic
Terrain depiction (if enabled and selected ON) and the FPS
movements.
When the SVS is installed and ON (Supplement 102) the display
format together with FPS assists the pilot to interpret, at first glance,
the aircraft’s path angle and make him aware of inadvertent descent
into land or water. If the SVS is not installed or OFF the FPS is still a
good vertical speed indication.
Expanded Pitch Tape is designed to be conformal to SVS 3D Terrain
depiction (when installed and selected on) and its aspect does not
change when SVS is OFF or not installed, to avoid abrupt changes of
Attitude Display Indication.

CURSOR CONTROL DEVICE (CC-701)
The Cursor Control Device (CCD) has been revised ergonomically
compare to previous phases of software to include a new joystick
which is used to move the display cursor through the MFD menu
selections and operate the MFD designator. There are two ENTER
buttons used for selecting an item currently highlighted by the cursor.
These are the center of the joystick, which is intended for use with the
thumb, and a dedicated button on top of the turret, which is intended
for use with the ring finger .
Also included on the CCD panel are SVS (if installed) select button
and CVS button (not active). See Figure 7-7.

INTERACTIVE NAVIGATION
The Interactive NAVigation (INAV) is a DB-based enhanced map
integrated into the Multi-Function Display (MFD) and selectable to
display the surrounding environment with respect to the aircraft
position and flight plan. The various options are available after
selecting the MAP or PLAN menu button and setting the TERRAIN,
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
AERONAUTICAL, GEOPOLITICAL and FLIGHT PLANS as required.
The feature provides enhanced graphical depiction of terrain,
obstacles, geopolitical boundaries and other elements as airways,
airspaces, airports, navaids, roads and railroads. See Figure 7-8 to
Figure 7-10.
INAV includes a 2-D representation of the terrain that can be displayed
inside the Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) of the PFD. This is
selected from the Display Controller WX/TERR button (Figure 7-11
and Figure 7-12) which toggles through the various options listed
below:
No press = No Weather or Terrain
1st press = Weather Radar (if installed)
2nd press = Absolute Terrain, SA Terrain, and Threat Terrain (If
EGPWS installed and functional)
3rd press = Absolute Terrain and Threat Terrain (if EGPWS
installed and functional)
4th press = No Weather (if Radar installed) or Terrain.
If EGPWS is installed, the Absolute Terrain layer is improved by
Situational Awareness and Threat Alert layers.

CUSTOM APPROACH
Custom Approach allows the pilot to build and fly a user defined
approach to the active flight plan destination, which could be either a
user defined waypoint or a waypoint from the NAV DB. Two different
approach definitions, (depending on the option files activated at
installation) may be selected from the MCDU CST APPR EDIT page:
— Custom approach without Level Segment: used for overland VFR
approaches.
The custom approach without the level segment comprises of IAF,
FAF, MAP, and MAH waypoints. These are shown in the vertical
and lateral profiles in Figure 7-14. The waypoints are temporary
so their idents are preceded by an asterisk.
The function uses VGP mode for vertical guidance during the
descent. The guidance will be along a descent vertical glide path
from the TOD to the MAP.
Page S101-36
Rev. 26

=== DOC PAGE 3759 ===
AW139 - RFM - 4D Supplement 101
Document N ° Phase 8 Additional
139G0290X002 Functions
— Custom approach with the Level Segment used for offshore
approaches (if option file installed).
The approach creates a lateral profile comprising of an initial
approach fix (IAF), final approach fix (FAF), bottom of descent
(BOD), missed approach point (MAP), and missed approach hold
(MAH) waypoints. These are shown in the vertical and lateral
profiles in Figure 7-15.
The function uses VRT mode for vertical guidance during the
descent. The VRT glideslope will be drawn to the BOD waypoint,
which is longitudinally offset from the MAP to create a level
segment prior to the MAP and to allow for deceleration and visual
location of the destination.
The VRT mode remains coupled during the descent to the BOD
then transitions to radio altitude hold (RHT) mode in order to flare
to the level segment. This happens when laterally sequencing the
BOD or when the capture criteria for RHT are met prior to the
BOD as determined by the flight director. The RHT mode remains
engaged at the MAP.
Note
If the approach information entered into the MCDU pages
produces an inappropriate approach profile the
conflicting parameters will be inverse video, on the
MCDU, and require modification.
For full information on the use of the Custom Approach refer Primus
FMS Phase 8 Pilot’s Manual, latest issue.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
Page S101-37
Rev. 26

GENERAL INFORMATION
The Primus EPIC Phase 8, when enabled via option file, allows the
selection of the Synthetic Vision System (SVS). This system enhances
flight crew awareness by providing a synthetic three dimensional view
of surrounding terrain, obstacles, runways and helipads on the
Primary Flight Display, in addition to standard flight instrument data.
The SVS uses terrain, obstacle and navigation databases to integrate
existing flight deck data with advanced symbology to assist in the
pilot’s ability to identify potential terrain and obstacle conflicts, as well
as to identify visual references.
An example of the PFD with SVS selected ON is shown in
Figure 1.
For full information on the use of the SVS refer Primus EPIC Phase 8
Avionics and AFCS Pilot’s Manual, latest issue.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S102-1

GENERAL
The Synthetic Vision System provides a three dimensional rendering
of terrain, obstacles, runway, helipad and approach symbology,
conformal to the actual aircraft position, altitude and attitude.
The SVS imagery, when selected on, acts as background for PFD
data.
The SVS is turned ON and OFF by selecting or deselecting the SVS
button on the CCD (Figure 7-1) or on the MCDU, selecting MENU and
the SVS page for SVS options. When the SVS is turned OFF, the
Blue-over-Brown display replaces the terrain on the PFD. An example
of the PDF with the SVS selected ON is shown in Figure 1.

selecting appropriate LSK in MCDU MENU.
The layout of the SVS page is shown in Figure 7-2. The following
selections are available:
L1 - Pushing L1 turns the FPRL OFF, AUTO or MAN.
L2 - Pushing L2 when FPRL is in Manual mode gives the pilot the
ability to adjust the value by turning the MCDU outer turn knob.
L5 - Adjusting the SVS terrain and HSI 2-D terrain brightness is done
by pushing L5 and using the MCDU outer turn knob.

SYNTHETIC SCENERY GENERAL
The terrain, obstacle, and airport databases have the following areas
of coverage:
• The terrain database has an area of coverage from North 80
degrees latitude to South 50 degrees latitude in all longitudes.
• The obstacle database has a worldwide area coverage for
reported obstacles taller than 100 feet (approximately 100,000
obstacles).
It should be noted that the inclusion of all such obstacles is not
guaranteed.
• The airport database has a worldwide area coverage for airports
with runways longer than 2,000 feet (approximately 8,600
airports and 30,000 runways).

CAUTION
The SVS display is intended to enhance terrain and
obstacle awareness. The display and database may not
provide the accuracy and fidelity on which to base routine
navigation decisions and plan routes to avoid terrain or
obstacles.
FLIGHT PATH REFERENCE LINE
The Flight Path Reference Line (FPRL) offers a terms of reference to
compare the aircraft Flight Path Symbol (FPS). It can be selected via
MCDU - SVS page and set manually or, for approaches, retrieved
automatically from FMS.
SVS Path Mode
Path-based mode offers a PFD representation prioritizing the display
of aircraft path, as represented by FPS. The FPS appears as a large
green symbol on the ADI. Cyclic Flight Director cues are referenced to
the FPS. A digital readout of Radar Height is placed close to the FPS,
when lower than 2500 ft. Significant split between FPS and ARS are
displayed via the use of Vertical Centering function.
SVS Pitch Mode
Pitch-based mode offers a traditional PFD representation, with
reduced emphasis on aircraft path. The FPS appears as a small white
symbol on the ADI. Cyclic Flight Director cues are referenced to the
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters ARS. A digital readout of Radar Height is placed close to the ARS,
when lower than 2500 ft. Vertical Centering is inactive, except for the
CAT A pre-push function.
Page S102-15
Rev. 26

SCENERY ORIENTATION
The three main symbols are overlaid on the SVS are the Zero Pitch
Reference Line (ZPRL), the Aircraft Reference Symbol (ARS) and the
Flight Path Symbol (FPS). Together with the pitch ladder, the ARS and
ZPRL give an immediate indication of the pitch attitude. The
combination of FPS and ZPRL give an immediate indication of vertical
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
speed while FPS and SVS provide immediate feedback about the
flight path with respect to represented scene, being the FPS
conformal. The FOV sector lines (frustum lines) on the HSI indicate
the sector that corresponds to the SVS lateral FOV, see Figure 7-4.
LATERAL TERRAIN CENTRING
In order to provide the best visual representation to enhance the
crew's situational awareness, depending upon the flight condition, the
SVS automatically selects the lateral centering among three different
modes: Track (TRK), Heading (HDG) and Split (SPL).
The basic mode for forward flight is the Track mode, which laterally
centres the SVS representation on the aircraft track. In low speed and
hover conditions, Heading mode is used instead, centering the SVS
representation on the aircraft heading. The Split mode supports
smooth transitions between HDG and TRK modes.
The actual centering mode is indicated on the left of the ADI, right of
the airspeed tape, via a dedicated annunciation, as shown in
Figure 7-3.
The lateral mode annunciator is boxed when the mode is steady,
flashing three times at the start of a mode transition and is unboxed
when transitioning between different modes. The unboxed label
indicates a hybrid situation in which the SVS is neither TRK nor HDG
centred.
Aircraft track and heading are represented by a single full or hollow
triangle respectively on the Zero Pitch Reference Line (ZPRL). In case
of high sideslip angles, these references can be shown dashed while
parked laterally on the ZPRL to indicate that they are no longer
conformal to the scene. In TRK the Flight Path Symbol (FPS) is
always centred in the display (allowed to move up and down to
indicate the flight path angle), while in HDG mode the FPS is
removed.
Page S102-16
Rev. 26

=== DOC PAGE 3789 ===
AW139 - RFM - 4D Supplement 102

The lateral terrain centring is the centring of SVS re-positioning along
from TRK centred to HDG centred or vice versa, during the mode
changes. As stated above, this is indicated by a label on the ADI as
shown in Figure 7-3. The label is boxed when the mode is steady,
flashing three times at the start of a mode transition and unboxed
when the transition is not yet complete.
Note that an unboxed label indicates a hybrid situation in which the
SVS is not TRK or HDG centred.
In TRK mode, the Field of View sector lines (so-called frustum) on the
HSI indicate the sector that corresponds to the SVS lateral FOV, see
Figure 7-4.

VERTICAL TERRAIN CENTRING
The FPS indicates the aircraft path angle with respect to the ZPRL
and the aircraft path with respect to the scene represented by SVS.
Whenever the SVS is set to Path Mode, the vertical terrain centring
technique is used to maximize the availability of path angle
information and to allow FPS remaining conformal to SVS as much as
possible.
This is achieved by moving the ARS, the pitch tape and the ZPRL up
or down as a group, together with represented terrain scene.
For downward movements of FPS, after the FPS has moved down to
the top of the HSI, it continues to move down to towards its lower limit,
pushing the HSI down as well as causing the removal of VHF, NAV
and XPDR tuning boxes. NO PFD TUNING is displayed, in this
condition radios will be tunable via MCDU only. Once the HSI has
reached its maximum down position, the FPS will then start to push
the SVS and ARS up (at a very slow rate).
Once the HSI has reached its maximum downward location, the ARS,
the ZPRL the pitch tape and SVS scene (if selected ON) will move up
as a group. After the push down condition is removed, due to FPS
Page S102-18
Rev. 26

=== DOC PAGE 3791 ===
AW139 - RFM - 4D Supplement 102
Document N ° Synthetic Vision
139G0290X002 System (SVS)
returning up, the ARS, the ZPRL pitch scale and SVS scene will return
to their original position (at a very slow rate) and the VHF, NAV and
XPDR tuning boxes will re-appear.
For upward FPS movement, after the FPS has reached its upper limit,
the ARS, the ZPRL, the pitch tape and the SVS scene (if selected ON)
will move down at a very slow rate to continue to display the FPS
conformal to the SVS. After the high FPA condition is removed, the
FPS will descend and the ARS, the ZPRL, the pitch tape and the SVS
scene (if selected ON) will return to their original position (at a very
slow rate).
Note the FPS may be displayed dashed when at the top or bottom of
the display to indicate that it is no longer conformal to the scene.
CAT A PRE-PUSH
In order to provide the best visual cues, room for the FPS on the pitch
tape and prevent SVS movement during a dynamic manoeuvre as
CAT A, when CAT A is selected for display (NF switch set to 102%
and CAT A button pressed on collective’s grip), the ARS and the HSI
will be pre-pushed down. At deselection of the CAT A, the ARS returns
to their standard location within 3 sec while the HSI returns within
30 sec.
SCENERY SYMBOLOGY
GRID LINES
Grid lines are regularly spaced semi-transparent black lines overlaying
the synthetic terrain. The grid lines run approximately North/South and
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
East/West and are spaced at approximately 0.1 NM by 0.1 NM for
terrain up to 2500 ft (820 m) and 0.4 NM by 0.4 NM for terrain beyond.
They follow the contour of the terrain.
The grid lines are hidden when higher terrain is near the aircraft
viewpoint as appropriate. The grid lines fade as they extend away
from the aircraft viewpoint.
Page S102-19
Rev. 26

=== DOC PAGE 3792 ===
Supplement 102 AW139 - RFM - 4D
Synthetic Vision Document N°
System (SVS) 139G0290X002
RANGE RINGS
The terrain image on the PFD is displayed with a set of curves labeled
with their distance from the aircraft. Range rings are white in color and
are displayed at 3 NM, 5 NM, 10 NM, and 20 NM from the aircraft
position.
The range rings follow the contour of the terrain and are masked by Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
the foreground terrain. Range rings are labeled with their distance
from the aircraft and are displayed to the right of the airspeed tape and
to the left of the aircraft pitch reference symbol.
RUNWAYS
The runway environment is comprised of the runway, displaced area,
stopway, and runway shoulder. The runway pavement can contain the
following markings.
Runway marking locations are estimated using the navigation
database. Since they are being estimated, the markings are given a
distinctive nonrealistic look so that while they give the pilot reference
information about the runway surface, it is still apparent to the pilot
that the runway markings on the PFD do no represent the physical
markings on the runway pavement.
All runways that are in the navigation database are displayed on the
PFD.
Runways are displayed at the width, length, and location indicated by
the navigation database with a minimum width of 40 feet.
The FMS-selected arrival runway is shown on the PFD with a cyan
colour. Runways that are not the FMS-selected arrival runway are not
highlighted.
Extended Arrival Runway Centerline
The extended arrival runway centerline is a dashed line originating
from the FMS-selected arrival runway that extends out 20 NM,
providing the pilot with improved visual alignment with the inbound
course.

Rev. 26

Airport Symbols and Runways
An airport symbol is displayed as a cyan box around the FMS-
selected arrival runway. The size of the airport symbol is exaggerated
when it comes into view to aid in locating it. As the aircraft moves
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
toward the airport, the size is decreased. When 3 NM from the airport,
the symbol is displayed to frame the runway. The runway length is
justified to the threshold end of the runway longitudinally and centered
on it laterally.

Helipad Symbol
The helipad symbol is made of a circular textured surface and a "H" in
the center. The location and radius of the helipad are retrieved from
the Navigation Database. When a helipad elevation is over 25 feet the
symbol is displayed on a pedestal, See Figure 7-6.

OBSTACLES
When EGPWS (Supplement 81) is installed, threats are represented
on SVS terrain and obstacles.
The EGPWS determines areas of terrain that are threats to the aircraft
due to either the terrain itself or obstacles that are located on the
terrain. Terrain and obstacles in the SVS image that are within a threat
area will be colored yellow (for caution) or red (for warning) as
appropriate to provide a visual alert to the pilot.

139G0290X002 Stowage Boxes
GENERAL INFORMATION
The Cabin Stowage Boxes consists of three different types of stowage
boxes (tall, medium and low) that can be mounted in the cabin
passenger compartment. The position of boxes mounted are only
compatible with certain cabin seating configurations and the stowage
box is installed after removal of passenger seats.
The boxes are intended for stowage of non- dangerous goods (as per
ICAO ANNEX 18).
The three sizes of baggage stowage boxes are shown in Figure 1 to
Figure 3.
The boxes are designed to attach to the standard seat rails in Row 1
and Row 2.
The box types are:
— Tall Stowage box, P/N 8G5010A24532
— Medium Stowage box, P/N 8G5010A24732
— Low Stowage box, P/N 8G5010A33432.
The Tall and Medium boxes have a door panel with a handle that,
when rotated anti-clockwise 90°, unlocks and allows the door to be
opened and removed. The closing procedure is the reverse of the
opening procedure. When closed and the handle rotated clockwise
the door is locked closed, see Figure 4.
An additional fixed handle is also mounted on the boxes which can be
used as a hand hold for passengers moving around the cabin.
The Low boxes have a top panel with a handle that when rotated
anticlockwise the panels are unlocked and can be raised and slid on
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
the rails to open. When shut and rotated clockwise the door panel is
locked, Figure 5.
The Cabin Stowage Boxes have front and side openings to allow fire
extinguisher discharge inside the container, in case of fire.
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S103-1
Rev. 28

139G0290X002 Stowage Boxes
SECTION 1 - LIMITATIONS
WEIGHT AND CENTER OF GRAVITY LIMITATIONS
After installation of the Cabin Stowage Boxes kit, the new empty
weight and center of gravity position must be determined.
CABIN CONFIGURATIONS LIMITATIONS
— A minimum of 3 seats, in at least one row, must be installed.
— In Row 1 a maximum of 2 stowage boxes may be installed, if the
seat configuration permits.
— In Row 2 a maximum of 1 stowage box may be installed when the
seat configuration permits.
When installed the Row 3 seat directly behind the stowage box (if
installed) must be removed.
— The stowage boxes must only be installed between BL -482.6 mm
and BL +482.6 mm, in order to not interfere with an emergency
exit.
— When the Mission Console is installed and a Row 2 stowage box
is required it must be installed on the opposite side of the cabin
with respect to the mission console position.
CABIN STOWAGE BOX LIMITATIONS
Only non-dangerous items may be stored in the cabin stowage boxes
as per ICAO Annex 18.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters Occupants must be present, seated in a position which permits them
to have full access to the door of each loaded cabin stowage box.
Stowage box (bin) doors must be closed and locked during Taxiing,
Take-Off, Flight and Landing.
Opening of any stowage box in flight is not permitted except for an
emergency to tackle a suspected fire within the stowage box.
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S103-13
Rev. 28

Note
In accordance with E.A.S.A procedures, the balance data
of this Section are not subject to E.A.S.A. approval.

loading the rotorcraft within approved limits of center of
gravity and on maintaining the loading within such limits.
NON DANGEROUS CARGO

non-flammable, non-breakable, non-toxic, non-explosive and inert.

INTRODUCTION
GENERAL INFORMATION
The supplement covers the installation in the cabin of Corporate
passenger seats VIP passenger.
P/N 4G2520F29011 Row 1
This configuration has up to 4 corporate seats installed in Row 1
(Refer Figure 1). Row 2 and Row 3, as already available (basic RFM
or Supplement 45) may be installed with the Coporate seats in Row 1.
Cabin Stowage boxes may also be installed (Refer Supplement 103).
P/N 4G2520F28911 Row 3
This configuration has up to 3 VIP seats installed in Row 3 (Refer
Figure 1). The Row 1 corporate seat configuration P/N 4G2520F29011
may be installed or Row 1 seats, as already available (basic RFM or
Supplement 45) may be installed with the VIP seats in Row 1. The
Mission Console Supplement configuration (Supplement 38) or the
Cabin Stowage boxes (Supplement 103) may also be installed.
Row 2 configurations cannot be installed.
Additional Kits Installed with the VIP Seat Installations
When the VIP Seat installation is fitted the following additional kits
options may also be installed:
The box types are:
— P/N 4G2520F29111, lower covers with stowage pockets for the 4,
Row 1 seats P/N 4G2520F29011.

seats, when required.
— P/N 4G2520F01411, life jackets installed below the 3, Row 3
seats, when required.

139G0290X002 Extension STN 7200
INTRODUCTION
GENERAL INFORMATION
This Supplement covers the Cabin Full Tunnel Extension (tunnel
above/between fuel tanks) and the Cabin Partial Tunnel Extension.
The installation has a dividing panel at STN 7200 mm to separate the
tunnel from the baggage area. The installation allows crew access into
these areas, as required, up to the dividing panel.
Cabin Full Tunnel Extension P/N 4G5338F00311
The modification consists of the removal of the cabin dividing panel
from STN 5700 mm and the installation of a panel at STN 7200 mm
and floor panel, mounted in the tunnel, with tie down rings and
restraint nets.
The new area exposed after the removal of the partition panel at STN
5700 mm allows the space above/between the main fuel tanks and
into the front part of the baggage bay from STN 5700 mm to 7200 mm
to be used as a storage area. Four Loading Areas with tie down rings
and dedicated net assemblies are available and all may be used. See
Figure 1.
Mounted on both side walls of the tunnel are two rails which can be
used to attach items.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
E.A.S.A. Approved Page S105-1
Rev. 30

LONGITUDINAL AUXILIARY FUEL TANK (P/N 4G2800F00111)
The Longitudinal Auxiliary Fuel Tank is a single additional fuel tank.
The tank consists of a fuel cell installed on the left hand side of the bay
above the standard fuel tanks. (See Figure 2) The tank is connected to
the left hand part of the main fuel tank and forms an extension to the
main fuel tank through one connector. It is filled via the main tank and
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
feeds the main tank by gravity. A fuel vent line from the tank is
connected to the main tank vent line system and an electrical
connection provides Fuel Gauging Control Unit information. The Fuel
Gauging System automatically compensates for the additional fuel
quantity.
Page S105-4 E.A.S.A. Approved
Rev. 30

SECTION 7 - SYSTEM DESCRIPTION
The High Intensity Strobe Light (HISL) installation configures the
aircraft with a dual colour white/red strobe light under the belly of the
aircraft (Figure 106-1) which is in addition to the standard red strobe
light mounted on the top of the fin. The white HISL emits a light at an
intensity of 2000 candela and is designed to increase the visibility of
the helicopter in daylight conditions. The red light is of lower intensity.
Pilot selection of the light is through the Anticollision switch (A/COLL)
on the Overhead panel with the following selections:
• BOTH (the fin mounted red upper light and the lower HISL light
illuminated)
• OFF (all anticollision lights unpowered)
• UPPER (the fin mounted red upper anticollision light
illuminated)
The selection of the HISL Light colour is using an additional switch on
the Overhead panel SEC A/COLL MODE with the following selections:
- RED
- WHITE
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
Refer Figure 106-2 for switch positions.
When the lighting MODE switch is on NVG mode (if installed) the
WHITE mode of the HISL is inhibited.

SECTION 6
WEIGHT AND BALANCE
Note
In accordance with E.A.S.A. procedures, the detail weight
and balance data of this Section are not subject to
E.A.S.A. approval.
The loading instructions of this Section, however, have
been accepted by E.A.S.A. as satisfying all requirements
for instructions on loading of the rotorcraft within approved
limits of weight and center of gravity, and on maintaining
the loading within such limits.
GENERAL
This Section provides information for the weight and balance compu-
tation of the AW139 helicopter.
It is the pilot's responsibility to ensure that the helicopter is properly
loaded to maintain for the duration of the flight the center of gravity
within the limitations defined in Section 1 of the Rotorcraft Flight Man-
ual.
Figures, charts and examples are provided to assist the pilot in com-
puting the proper loading conditions.

COMPUTATION OF LOADING
LONGITUDINAL LOADING EXAMPLES
The empty weight and the moment of the AW139 helicopter can be
found in Chart B (Helicopter Weighing Record).
The values in Chart B are obtained by weighing the aircraft and com-
puting the empty weight, moment and CG.
Subsequently as items of equipment are added or removed, entries
shall be made in Chart C (Basic Weight and Balance Record) and the
new empty weight and balance computed.
The empty weight includes fixed ballast, hydraulic fluid, transmission
oil, engine oil and unusable fuel.
Three sample loadings are shown below (in the sample loading the
empty weight and CG arm are assumed to be 3700 Kg and 5500 mm).

WEIGHT AND BALANCE DETERMINATION
Instructions for weight and balance determination are herewith
enclosed with instructions for use of charts to enable the operator to
obtain all necessary data as to basic helicopter configuration, empty
weight and center of gravity. These charts will also provide for continu-
ous control of weight and balance of the helicopter.
This system of weight and balance computation requires the use of
charts and forms. They are identified as follows:
Chart A - Equipment List.
Chart B - Helicopter Weighing Record.
Chart C - Basic Weight and Balance Record.
Chart D - Data for Helicopter Weight and Balance Computation
Chart E - Weight and Balance Computation
WEIGHT AND BALANCE DATA RESPONSIBILITY
The aircraft manufacturer inserts all helicopter identifying data on the
various charts. This record constitutes the basic weight and balance
data of the helicopter, to which the Rotorcraft Flight Manual was
assigned, for the condition shown on chart A. The operator shall keep
this data up-to-date by recording all changes made to the configura-
tion of the helicopter.
HELICOPTER WEIGHING
The helicopter must be weighed:
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
1. When major modifications or repairs are made, or kits are installed
/removed.
2. When the basic weight data is suspected to be an error.
3. At time of major overhaul.
4. In accordance with E.A.S.A. instructions.
Page 6-15

=== DOC PAGE 3880 ===
Section 6 AW139 - RFM - 4D
Weight and Balance Document N°
139G0290X002
USE OF CHARTS AND FORMS
USE OF CHART A
The Chart A gives the weight, arm and moment of all the standard and
optional equipment. The manufacturer of the helicopter places check
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
marks in the “Basic Configuration” column to identify the items of
equipment in the helicopter for the weighing condition. A check (V) in
the columns headed “In Helicopter” indicates the presence of the item
in the helicopter, and a zero (0) indicates its absence. The next col-
umns of chart A will permit inspection of the helicopter for equipment
actually installed. When making an inventory, note whether any items
of equipment have been installed or removed and if so enter corre-
sponding weight and moment change on Chart C.
Subsequent check list inventories shall be carried out in the following
cases:
1. When the helicopter undergoes modification, major repair or
overhaul.
2. When changes in equipment are made for a different type of
operation.
3. When the helicopter is reweighed.
WEIGHING INSTRUCTIONS
Preliminary instructions
1. Remove dirt, grease, moisture, etc. from the helicopter.
Note
The helicopter must be weighed in a closed hangar.
2. Drain fuel from tanks.
Page 6-16

=== DOC PAGE 3881 ===
AW139 - RFM - 4D Section 6
Document N° Weight and Balance
139G0290X002
Note
If it is impossible to drain fuel due to fire hazard or local
regulations, fill fuel tanks to capacity. Since the weight of
fuel varies with temperature, determine actual specific
gravity by use of a hydrometer. Multiply by tank capacity to
obtain total fuel weight. Never weigh with partially filled
tanks.
3. Always keep oil reservoirs filled.
4. Fill main transmission to normal level.
5. Fill hydraulic fluid reservoirs to normal level.
6. Conduct an inventory of the operating equipment actually installed
in the helicopter by means of Chart A.
Weighing procedure
(Figure 6-3)

31 of Maintenance Manual.
2. Make sure that weighing equipment is zeroed.
3. Connect each cell (1) to the scales equipment.
4. Let each cell (1) and the scales indications become stable.
5. Record the weights shown on the scales for each cell. Make sure
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
that you record the related jack position for each weight.
6. Calculate the longitudinal and lateral Center of Gravity (CG)
positions.
7. Disconnect each cell (1) from the scales equipment.
8. Lower the helicopter.

USE OF CHART B
1. Enter the actual scale readings in the first column of sheet 1.
Subtract tare, if any, from the scale readings to obtain the net
weight.
2. Multiply the net weights by their respective arms. Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
3. Add the net weight and moments.
4. Divide the total moment by the net weight to obtain “as weighed”
CG position. Transfer the “TOTAL” (as weighed) weight arm and
moment to the sheet 2 of Chart B.
5. Subtract the total weight and moment of equipment weighed but
not part of the basic helicopter (list these items in column one).
6. Add the weight and moment of unusable fuel.
7. Add the total weight and moment of the basic items not in
helicopter when weighed (list these in column two). Added items
shall be marked on Chart A.
8. Enter the new basic weight and moment on Chart C.
USE OF CHART C
Chart C is a continuous history of the basic weight and moment result-
ing from modifications and equipment is considered the current weight
and balance status of the basic helicopter. Make additions or subtrac-
tions to the basic weight and moment in Chart C as follows:
1. When the helicopter undergoes modification, major repair or
overhaul.
2. When changes in equipment are made for a different type of
operation.
3. When the helicopter is reweighed.

Obtain the corresponding arms from Chart D and calculate the
moments.
3. Add weight and moments. Divide total moment by total weight to
obtain CG arm.

within allowable limits.

SECTION 7
SYSTEM DESCRIPTION
INTRODUCTION
This section provides a general description of the AW139 helicopter
and its systems.
HELICOPTER DESCRIPTION
The AW139 is a large size multi-purpose helicopter, powered by two
Pratt & Whitney PT6C-67C turbo-shaft engines. The helicopter has a
five-blade fully articulated main-rotor and a four-blade articulated tail-
rotor.
The structure is made up of three main modules: the cockpit, the cabin
and the tail-boom.
The cockpit includes the pilot (RH) and co-pilot (LH) seats. The seats
are installed side by side and are adjustable and crash-worthy.
The instrumentation is NVG compatible and the dual-controls are
adjustable. Two forward opening hinged-doors with an emergency
release give access to the cockpit on both sides. Large glass
windshields and clear acrylic windows in the crew doors, lower nose,
and roof area give the crew good visibility.
The cabin includes the passenger seats and the baggage-bay area at
the back of the fuselage. A full size plug-in sliding door is located on
each side of the cabin area. Each sliding door has two acrylic-plastic
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters windows, and can be secured in the open or closed position.
The seating arrangements can be changed depending on the
configuration:
Standard civil transport 12 passengers
High density civil transport 15 passengers
Civil EMS 4 litter patients, 2 non-litter patients
and 2 medical attendants
Page 7-1
Rev. 24

=== DOC PAGE 3910 ===
Section 7 AW139 - RFM - 4D
System Description Document N°
139G0290X002
The cockpit and the cabin have separate ventilation and heating sys-
tems with air-conditioning as an optional.
The tail-boom is attached to back of the fuselage and can be removed.
The tail-boom holds the tail-rotor and drive-train, the vertical fin and
the horizontal stabilizer.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters

INTEGRATED AVIONICS SYSTEM
(PRIMUS EPIC SYSTEM)
INTRODUCTION
®
The PRIMUS EPIC system is an integrated avionics system that
includes the following sub-systems necessary to operate the helicop-
ter.
— Auto-Flight
— Communications
— Indicating and recording
— Navigation
— Central maintenance
The system can also integrate the communications and navigation
systems with other sub-systems of the helicopter.
GENERAL
®
The PRIMUS EPIC system is integrated into the Modular Avionics
Units (MAU), the Modular Radio Displays (MRC) and the flat panel
displays.
The software is integrated in different places under the Digital Engine
Operating System (DEOS). Mechanical and virtual controllers are
used to control the helicopter. The system includes a Maintenance
System to monitor the operation of the helicopter.
®
The AW139 PRIMUS EPIC system is available in two main configu-
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
rations:
— Single pilot VFR
— Dual pilot IFR
Both configurations use the same display formats, controllers and
sensors. The VFR configuration is a sub-system to the IFR configura-
tion.
Page 7-11

=== DOC PAGE 3920 ===
Section 7 AW139 - RFM - 4D
System Description Document N°
139G0290X002
Modular Avionics Unit (MAU)
The MAU is a cabinet that contains field-removable modules that inte-
grate the following equipment or systems.
— Power Supply Module (PSM)
— Network Interface Controller with Processor (NIC/PROC) Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
— Custom I/O (CSIO) module
— Control I/O (CIO) module
— Actuator I/O Processor (AIOP)
— Central Maintenance Computer (CMC)
— Database Module (DBM)
— Global Positioning System (GPS) (optional)
— Video CIO (optional)
AUTO-FLIGHT
The Automatic Flight Control System (AFCS) is controlled by the two
Modular Avionics Units (MAU) of the PRIMUS EPIC® avionics sys-
tem. The MAU’s process information for the AFCS and are connected
to the following components:
— The autopilot controller
— The guidance controller
— Linear-actuators
— Rotary trim actuators
— Air data modules
— Attitude and reference Systems
Page 7-12

=== DOC PAGE 3921 ===
AW139 - RFM - 4D Section 7
Document N° System Description
139G0290X002
The AFCS has the following two basic modes of operation:
— Attitude Retention mode(ATT)
— Stability Augmentation System mode (SAS).
The ATT retention mode permits long term stabilization for hands-off
flying and it can be coupled to the flight director commands. SAS
mode gives short-term damping for hands-on flying.
The Yaw control function is engaged automatically when the auto-pilot
is selected. The yaw control remains active in both ATT and SAS
mode. Dual yaw control is provided when both auto-pilots are
engaged.
The collective axis of the AFCS drives the helicopter collective con-
trols. The collective controls are linked to a parallel actuator and a
force feel assembly to give the pilot motive power and artificial feel.
The auto-trim system controls the linear actuators and keeps them in
their center-of-travel position. Pitch and roll auto-trim is functional
when one or both auto-pilots are engaged in any mode, except SAS
mode.
The autopilot controller
The autopilot controller permits the following functions:
— Engagement of the auto-pilots
— Selection of the auto-pilot mode
— Coupling of the auto-pilot to the flight director
— Selection of Pre-Flight Test Mode
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
The guidance controller
The guidance controller permits the selection of all the AFCS Flight
Director functions. The AFCS is controlled by the autopilot controller
that interfaces with the two MAU’s.
Page 7-13

=== DOC PAGE 3922 ===
Section 7 AW139 - RFM - 4D
System Description Document N°
139G0290X002
Linear-actuators
Six high-frequency smart linear-actuators provide limited control of the
pitch, roll and yaw axis. The linear actuators receive 28 V dc electrical
power directly from the aircraft power bus.
Rotary trim actuators
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
Three low-frequency rotary trim actuators provide full control of the
pitch, roll, yaw and collective axis.
Air data modules
Two Air Data Modules (ADM) supply static and dynamic pressure
information to the MAU’s
Attitude and reference Systems
Two Attitude and Reference Systems (AHRS) provide the MAU’s with
inner loop control and outer loop filter prediction where required.
Attitude Retention mode (ATT)
In the ATT mode (uncoupled), the autopilot pitch and roll channels are
engaged and will maintain the attitude of the helicopter. The ATT
mode will bring the helicopter back to its reference attitude after a dis-
turbance.
To make small changes to the pitch or roll attitude the pilot can use the
switch on the cyclic control lever. To make larger corrections the pilot
can use the Force Trim Correct (FTR) switch and make the changes
manually.
The pilot can override the AFCS ATT mode at any time by taking over
the controls manually.
In ATT mode, the autopilots pitch and roll channels can be coupled to
the Flight Director (FD) commands. This allows for Two-Cue operation
that lets the FD control the lateral (roll) and vertical (pitch) axis.
The collective channel is also coupled to the FD commands for Three-
Cue operations. Three-cue operation allows the FD to control the lat-
eral, vertical and collective (power) axis.
Page 7-14

=== DOC PAGE 3923 ===
AW139 - RFM - 4D Section 7
Document N° System Description
139G0290X002
The autopilot will couple to the FD if both autopilots are engaged in the
ATT mode and the FD modes are selected.
Stability Augmentation System mode (SAS)
SAS mode gives short-term damping of external aircraft disturbances
and improves the handling capabilities during hands-on flying. SAS
mode also gives yaw rate damping, low speed heading hold and auto-
matic turn co-ordination. SAS is intended for use where extensive air-
craft maneuvering is required and the pilot prefers to be hands-on
without attitude retention.
SAS is selected by pushing the SAS button on the auto-pilot controller.
When operating in SAS, the cyclic beep switches will not give attitude
reference changes but may still be used to set Flight Director (FD) ref-
erences. Because this is a hands-on control mode, the AFCS can be
operated with force trim ON or OFF.

The communication system contains the equipment for communicat-
ing in the helicopter, with other aircraft, and with ground stations.
The communication system includes the following sub-systems:
— Modular Radio System
— Audio Integrating System
— VHF AM/FM NAT NTX 138 radio installation (optional equipment)
Modular Radio System
The Modular Radio System includes the Modular Radio Cabinet
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters (MRC). The MRC uses modules from the PRIMUS EPIC® system that
supply Communication and Navigational data to the flight-crew. It con-
tains the standard navigation and communication systems, including
VOR, ILS, ADF DME and VHF communication, and the Mode-S tran-
sponder system.

NAVIGATION
®
The navigation system is integrated in the PRIMUS EPIC avionic
system and includes the following sub-systems:
— Flight Environmental Data
— Attitude and Direction
— Landing and Taxiing Aids
— Independent Position Determining
— Dependant Position Determining
— Flight Management Computing.
Flight enviromental data
The Flight Environmental Data system includes a primary and a sec-
ondary Air Data System (ADS).
The ADS uses air data probes to show the airspeed, outside air tem-
perature, altitude and static/pitot pressure on the Primary Flight Dis-
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
play.
Attitude and direction
The attitude and direction system supplies attitude heading reference
data to the flight-crew and includes the Attitude Heading Reference
System (AHRS).
The AHRS uses magnetic and inertial forces to measure and give the
attitude and direction of the helicopter.

Landing and taxiing aids
The Landing and Taxiing Aids receive data from ground installations
and include the following sub-systems:
— Radio Altimeter System
— VOR/ILS/Data Link (VIDL) System. Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
RADIO ALTIMETER SYSTEM
The Radio Altimeter System uses Frequency-Modulated Continuous
Wave (FMCW) signals to find the helicopters altitude during the
approach and landing stages of a flight. The Radio Altitude Data is
shown on the Primary Flight Displays.
VOR/ILS/DATA LINK SYSTEM (VIDL)
The VIDL system is part of the Modular Radio System and can oper-
ate in VOR, ILS and VDB mode.
The VOR receiver supplies bearing in degrees to and from the ground
station.
The ILS supplies approach and landing navigation data.
The VDB receiver supplies reception of GPS correction data and run-
way flight-paths for the GPS landing system.
Independent position determining
The Independent Position Determining system can determine the heli-
copters position without ground stations and/or orbital satellites. The
system includes the Weather Radar System (WX) and the Lightning
Sensor System (LSS).
The WX system identifies the location and intensity of rain and hail in
the helicopters flight-path. It includes a ground-map function that iden-
tifies the contour of the ground (terrain). The weather and terrain data
is shown on the Primary Flight Display (PFD) and the Multi Function
Display (MFD) units.
The LSS identifies the location and intensity of lightning in a radius of
5 to 100 NM of the helicopter. The LSS operates directly with the WX
system, the LSS data is shown on the PFDs and the MFDs.

Dependant position determining
The Dependant Position Determining system uses ground stations
and/or orbital satellites to find the helicopters position and velocity.
The Dependant Position Determining system is part of the Modular
Radio System and includes the following sub-systems:
— Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) System
— Air Traffic Control (ATC) Transponder (XPDR) System
— Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) System
— Global Positioning System (GPS)(optional).
DISTANCE MEASURING EQUIPMENT SYSTEM
The Distance Measuring Equipment supplies the data for in-flight nav-
igation, terminal navigation and area guidance. The system measures
the distance from the ground station, ground speed and time-to-sta-
tion. The Distance Measuring Equipment consists of a DME Module
and a dedicated DME antenna. The DME system is connected to the
display system and to the Flight Management System through the Avi-
onic Standard Communication Bus (ASCB-D).The digital audio bus
transmits the DME identification audio signals (IDENT) to each audio
panel in the audio system.
The DME system operates with radio pulses in the frequency range
from 960 MHz to 1215 MHz. The airborne system transmits from 1025
MHz to 1150 MHz to a ground station. The receiver frequency range is
from 962 MHz to 1213 MHz.
Indication
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters The PFD receives the distance data from the DME and displays the
distance indication in nautical miles to the left of the horizontal situa-
tion indicator (HSI). When the source of NAV data shown is DME-hold,
a DME H indication is shown adjacent to the distance indication. Indi-
cations that identify a DME station or FMS TO waypoint can also be
displayed adjacent to the distance indication.

AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL TRANSPONDER SYSTEM
The XS-856 Transponder Module has the encoding and decoding
capability to operate in Mode S that allows digital addressing of indi-
vidual aircraft and it is fundamental for the operation of the Optional Kit
Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS). It supports provision of
data and control to the TCAS* computer through an ARINC 429 link.
The XS-856 Transponder Module obtains barometric altitude data
from the air data functions on the Avionic Standard Communications
Bus (ASCB-D). The XS-856 Transponder connects to the display sys-
tem through the ASCB-D, following the same arrangement as the
other radio systems.
One XPDR, P/N 3G0630A00912, is included in the basic equipment
nd
configuration. The 2 XPDR P/N 3G3450F00512 is optional.
The Enhanced Mode S XPDR XS-858A P/N 7517401-960, which is
compliant with ICAO Doc 7030/4 Regional Supplementary Procedues
where Enhanced Surveillance is required, is an available option. With
this system the following parameters are transmitted: Magnetic Head-
ing, Indicated Air Speed, Barometric Altitude Rate, Roll Angle, True
Track Angle, Ground Speed, True Air Speed, Selected Altitude.

FMS AND GPS
FUNCTIONAL DESCRIPTION
The FMS combines the inputs of other aircraft systems (GPS, DME,
VOR, AHRS, ADS) to output navigation, lateral and vertical
commands, and aircraft performance predictions. FMS uses GPS as
long range sensor and DME/DME and VOR/DME as short range
sensors.
Primary functions of FMS are position computation and flight planning.
These functions work with the associated guidance in both lateral and
vertical axes. The FMS Database is essential to these functions in
order to easily retrieve, navaids, airways, procedures, airports, other
navigation data and store and retrieve waypoints and flight plans.
Performance is a secondary function containing fuel management,
time estimates for the flight, vertical navigation estimates, stored flight
plans and other functions.
Provided the FMS is receiving usable signals, it has been
demonstrated capable of and has been shown to meet the accuracy
specifications of:
— VFR/IFR en route domestic, terminal, and instrument approach
(GPS, VOR, VOR-DME, NDB, NDB-DME, RNAV) operation using
the WGS-84 (or NAD 83) coordinate reference datum in
accordance with the criteria of AC 25-11, AC 00-314, AC 20-130A.
Satellite navigation data is based upon use of only the Global
Positioning System (GPS) operated by the United States.
FMS DISPLAYS AND CONTROL PANELS

(HSI) and MCDU.

— A map presentation that shows:
• Radio navigation aids
• Airports

— Scratchpad
The bottom line on the MCDU display is the scratchpad. The
scratchpad is a working area where the pilot can enter data
and/or verify data before line selecting the data into its proper
position. Alphanumeric entries are made to the scratchpad
using the keyboard. As each key is pushed, the character is
displayed in the scratchpad. Information in the scratchpad
does not affect the FMS until it is moved to another line on the
display. Data is retained in the scratchpad throughout all mode
and page changes.

FMS DATA BASE
The FMS Database consists of two parts: a navigation database and a
custom (or pilot defined) database.
The navigation data base (NDB) can not be changed by the pilot.
Using the custom database the pilot can customize the FMS by
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
defining waypoints and storing flight plans.

The navigation database contains worldwide coverage of navaids,
airways, standard instrument departure/standard terminal arrival route

runways as following:
• Navaids (VOR, DME, ILS, MLS, NDB)
• Airports

• Runways
• Airways
• SIDs and STARs
• Approaches
• Named Intersections
• Outer Markers

flight plans. Up to 1000 pilot defined waypoints can be stored.
